extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent attorneys, and patent-office practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and procedural standards for preparing patent specifications and for related patent-office proceedings (caveats, petitions, oaths, fees, reissues, disclaimers). Focused on what must be described, formalities, and remedies for defective specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel combination versus mere improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a combination of parts existed before up to a given point, and the inventor's contribution merely takes up at that point and adds further combinations, then if the subsequent combinations alone are his invention the former combinations give him no right; if he has only invented an improvement of the old engine his specification claiming the whole will be bad. If, however, he has invented a machine consisting of a perfectly new conformation of parts (though all parts were used before), he is entitled to a patent for a new machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the invention is an improvement of an existing engine or a new engine by virtue of a new conformation of parts; if only an improvement, claiming the whole machine is objectionable and will render the specification bad. Jury/verdict implications illustrated by the Browne example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description sufficiency for methods and principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle cannot be the object of a patent. A method merely as such is not a proper subject unless the patent is in fact granted for tangible means of carrying that method into practice. If a method is claimed, the description must be very accurate: so clear and evident that no experiments are necessary to learn it and to put it in practice as beneficially as the patentee enjoys it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat descriptions of methods like descriptions of manufactures or machines: provide tangible means and such accuracy/detail that a skilled person needs no experimentation to practice the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification requirements for chemical discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: When a chemical discovery is the foundation of the invention, the substance (not the principle) ought to be described. The ingredients, their proportions, the time of mixing, &c. ought to be fully stated, and then the beneficial use to which the substance can be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full recipe-like disclosure: ingredients, proportions, timing, procedure, and stated uses so the public can make and use the substance as the patentee does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full and exact disclosure of new manufactures and parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part which is new, however minute, must be clearly described. In specifications of a substance, the simplest elements and the best modes of making and using it must be accurately stated. In descriptions of machines there must, with scrupulous fidelity, be set forth the cheapest materials, the most exact proportions of the parts, the most expeditious and the best mode of conducting them, with the precise times of putting on or taking off any part of the machine; and an improvement or new combination must be kept distinctly apart from the old manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose best modes, materials, exact proportions, timings, and separate the new improvement from prior manufacture. The public must be put in possession in a way as ample and beneficial as the patentee enjoys it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of claiming known matter and statutory disclaimer/remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: It was a technical rule that if the inventor claims anything in the title or specification which is not new, the whole patent became void. The Act (5 & 6 William IV c.83) altered this: a grantee may enter a disclaimer of any part of the title or specification, stating the reason, or enter a memorandum of any alteration not extending the exclusive right; disclaimers or alterations, when filed and enrolled, are deemed part of the letters-patent/specification in all courts. Caveats may be entered against such disclaimers/alterations; the attorney-general/solicitor-general may require advertisement of the disclaimer. The entry of a disclaimer under this Act does not give a right of action for infringements committed previously to the disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If non-new material is claimed, use statutory mechanisms (disclaimer/memorandum of alteration) rather than risking entire patent invalidation. Be aware of caveat rights, advertising requirements, and limitations of using disclaimers as retroactive cures for past infringements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat for incomplete invention: who may file and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Any citizen (or qualifying alien) who has invented a new art, machine, or improvement and desires more time to mature it may file a caveat on payment of twenty dollars. The caveat must set forth the design and purpose thereof, and its principal and distinguishing characteristics, and is filed in the confidential archives and preserved in secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A caveat protects priority while maturing an invention; include principal/distinguishing characteristics. The $20 fee counts toward later patent fees if a patent is taken out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat interference procedure and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: If another person applies for a patent within one year for an invention which may in any respect interfere with the caveat, the commissioner must deposit the application materials in confidential archives and give notice by mail to the caveat filer, who then has three months after notice to file description, specifications, drawings, and model; if specifications of claim interfere, like proceedings to interfering applications may follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a caveat triggers a statutory notice/response procedure and can lead to interference proceedings; ensure timely filing of full materials upon notification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and content of the petition/application
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must make application in writing to the Commissioner of Patents (historically by petition, generally with the specification annexed). The form of the petition is not material provided it sets forth the facts to which the applicant is required to make oath. When filed, it is presumed to adopt the specification filed at the same time and to ask for a patent for the invention therein described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Patent Office rule forms where advisable, but ensure the petition includes all facts needed for the statutory oath and references the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath of the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant is required to make oath or affirmation that he does verily believe that he is 'the original and first inventor' and that he does not know or believe that the same was ever before known or used, and also of his country of citizenship; the oath may be made before any authorized person. The oath is of belief (not absolute knowledge): if he believed himself first inventor when taking the oath, subsequent discovery that it was known elsewhere (but not described/patented publicly) does not invalidate the patent. Irregularity in form of the oath may be cured by issuance of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the applicant truthfully swears belief of being original inventor and states citizenship; the oath places onus probandi on challengers once recited in the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment of fees before consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Before an application is considered by the commissioner, the applicant shall pay into the U.S. Treasury the sum of thirty dollars if a citizen (or qualifying resident alien), or five hundred dollars if a subject of the King of Great Britain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay required fees at time of filing/application; fee amounts differ by nationality (historical amounts shown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signatures, seals, and correction of clerical mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents shall be issued in the name of the United States, under the seal of the office, signed by the Secretary of State and countersigned by the Commissioner of Patents. The Secretary's sanction to a correction of a clerical mistake may be given in writing afterwards; the commissioner may correct the copy to conform to the original. If the mistake in the enrolled patent is material, the letters operate only after correction, but clerical corrections may operate back to the original date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal signatures/seals are required; clerical errors can often be corrected administratively, but material errors have limited retroactive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue/renewal for defective or insufficient specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective or insufficient description or specification, or by claiming more than the patentee had right to claim, and the error arose by inadvertence, accident, or mistake without fraudulent intent, the commissioner may, upon surrender of the patent and payment of fifteen dollars, cause a new patent to be issued to the inventor for the residue of the unexpired term in accordance with the patentee's corrected description and specification. In case of death or assignment, the right vests in executors, administrators, or assignees. The reissued patent and corrected specification have the same effect in law as if originally filed in corrected form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surrender-and-reissue to cure inadvertent defects or overbroad claims (non-fraudulent). Pay the statutory $15 and follow the statutory recording/annexing procedures. Reissue is a statutory remedy but commissioner review and revision of claims applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annexation of subsequent improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee desirous of adding the description and specification of any new improvement invented subsequent to the date of his patent may, with like proceedings as for original applications and on payment of fifteen dollars, have the same annexed to the original description and specification; the commissioner shall certify the time of annexation and record it, and it shall have the same legal effect as if embraced originally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annex improvements by formal filing and payment; annexed improvements become part of the patent record and are effective as of their recording as certified by the commissioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's revision, restrictions, and applicant remedies on reissue/addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever application is made for an addition of a newly-discovered improvement or for re-issue, the specification of claim annexed shall be subject to revision and restriction in the same manner as original applications. The commissioner will not add the improvement or grant re-issue until the applicant has entered a disclaimer or altered his specification of claim in accordance with the commissioner's decision; the applicant, if dissatisfied, shall have the same remedy and privileges as in original applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect examination and possible requirement to disclaim or amend claims on reissue/annexation; administrative decision subject to statutory review remedies but commissioner has primary authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality of commissioner's decision on surrender/reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision of the Commissioner in respect to surrendering an old patent and granting a new one is not reexaminable elsewhere unless it appears on the face of the patent that he exceeded his authority and there is a clear repugnancy between the old and the new patent or the new one has been obtained by collusion between the commissioner and the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioner's discretionary acts on surrender/reissue are presumptively conclusive; courts will not reexamine absent clear excess of authority or collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and scope of a renewed patent
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent is renewed (reissued), it is granted for the unexpired term commencing from the date of the original patent which is surrendered, and consequently operates from the commencement of the original and will enure to the benefit of assignees who became such before the renewal. An inventor in a renewed patent may omit a part of his original invention and retain only what he deems fit to retain; a renewed patent claiming less than the original may nevertheless be valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue dates back to the original grant for term computation and benefits prior assignees; patentees may narrow claims/omit parts in renewal without necessarily injuring their rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers to cure overbroad claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications may be amended by filing a disclaimer whenever, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, the original claim was too broad, claiming more than that of which the patentee was the original or first inventor, provided some material and substantial part of the thing patented is justly and truly his own. Such a disclaimer may be filed in the patent office by the patentee, his administrator, executors, and assigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File statutory disclaimers to narrow overbroad claims (non-fraudulent situations) to preserve the valid portion of the patent; disclaimers can be entered by the patentee or successors.
